title: TC0-12032
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a Mexican citizen who alleges that he fears being harmed in Mexico by members of an organized crime group who killed his half-sister. He further alleges that he fears he would be harmed because of threats made by a former work supervisor in Canada after the Appellant reported this man's unlawful activities. The Appellant came to Canada in XXXX 2019 and made a claim for refugee protection in October 2019.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) heard the Appellant's claim on September 23, 2020 and rejected it on October 28, 2020. The determinative issues were credibility, delay in making a claim, and internal flight alternative (IFA).
The Appellant argues that the RPD made unreasonable and incorrect findings and failed to properly consider the evidence when applying the IFA test.1 DECISION
I dismiss the appeal. The determinative issue is IFA. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The Appellant seeks to rely on new evidence in this appeal.2 He has submitted an Affidavit, sworn by the Appellant on December 23, 2020.3

According to the law,4 I can accept the evidence only if: i. it arose after the RPD decision; or ii. it was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to provide it before the decision.
If the evidence meets at least one of these requirements, I must decide that the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.5

I admit the Affidavit as new evidence. In his Affidavit, the Appellant states that on December 10, 2020 he was informed that his former work supervisor, XXXX, was asking for his contact information and is upset about business losses for which he blames the Appellant. The evidence in the Affidavit arose after the date of the RPD's decision so it is admissible under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).6 It is new and I find that it passes the threshold for credibility and is relevant to the Appellant's claim because he alleges that XXXX is an agent of harm. No oral hearing

The Appellant has requested an oral hearing.7 He argues that the hearsay evidence in his Affidavit is based on his information and belief and should be admitted and tested for credibility at an oral hearing. The Appellant argues that the evidence raises a serious issue as to his credibility and that it is central to the decision on his claim because it demonstrates a continued interest in the Appellant by an alleged agent of persecution and would potentially justify accepting the claim.8 I am not persuaded by the Appellant's argument.

Although the new evidence has the potential to support the Appellant's allegation that he fears XXXX and that XXXX is interested in him, acceptance of this evidence would not justify allowing or rejecting the claim. I accept that the Appellant has heard that XXXX has asked for his contact information, that he is upset with the Appellant, and that there are rumours about the Appellant's involvement in the investigation of a workplace in southwestern Ontario. I find no discrepancies in the evidence that I would need to ask the Appellant about, as a matter of procedural fairness. I am able to consider and weigh the new evidence without an oral hearing. Evidence of XXXX interest in contacting the Appellant could not be determinative of the claim, given that the Appellant has presented no evidence that XXXX has connections to anyone in Mexico who could harm the Appellant.9 If the Appellant has other evidence that supports his allegation that XXXX would harm him in Mexico, he could have applied to present it as new evidence. He has not done so.

I do not find that the Appellant's Affidavit raises a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility that would justify allowing or rejecting his claim.10 Therefore, the request for an oral hearing is denied.
The role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is to look at all the evidence and decide whether the RPD made the correct decision.11 ANALYSIS

paragraphs.text: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida or Campeche. As IFA is the determinative issue, I will address those of the Appellant's arguments that pertain to the viability of the IFA. This includes the arguments aimed at four credibility concerns expressed by the RPD. The legal test for IFA

There are two prongs to the legal test for a viable IFA.12 The first prong requires that there be no serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, no risk under section 97 of the IRPA, meaning no danger of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

The second prong requires that conditions in the IFA be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including personal circumstances, for the claimant to go and live there. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location.13 The RPD correctly found that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a section 97 risk in Merida or Campeche

The RPD concluded that the Appellant did not establish that he would face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture, if he relocated to Merida or Campeche.14 The Appellant argues that this is incorrect.15 I find no error in the RPD's conclusion. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established that an IFA is not viable on the basis of the first prong of the test. My reasons follow. The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that cartel members are motivated to pursue him

The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence to support a finding that the Appellant is being pursued by cartel members.16 The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored evidence that he has been targeted by people connected to a criminal group.17 On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that people connected to a cartel or organized crime group are motivated to pursue him.

I accept, for purposes of the analysis, that the Appellant's sister was violently attacked and killed in XXXX 2017 in Chiapas.18 The RPD's finding that the Appellant failed to establish that he was being pursued by cartel members flowed from a series of credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence. The Appellant argues that these credibility concerns lack merit.19 I am not persuaded by his arguments. The Appellant's credibility is undermined by his speculation about the cartels

The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant's inconsistent and speculative evidence about who is responsible for killing his sister.20 The Appellant acknowledges that his testimony naming two cartels was speculative. He argues that this should not undermine the fact that there is evidence indicating that individuals who threatened him were part of a criminal organization in Mexico.21 This argument rests on assuming that it has been established as a fact that the Appellant has been threatened and that the only issue is the identity of those who threatened him. The assumption is unfounded. The onus is on the Appellant to establish that he faces a threat by presenting credible evidence. The Appellant further argues that it may be impossible to know which group is targeting him. Again, this argument rests on the assumption that the Appellant is being targeted. The RPD found that the Appellant failed to establish that he was targeted. This finding was based, in part, on a credibility concern arising out of his speculation as to the identity of the alleged agent of persecution. I find no error in the RPD's assessment of this evidence.

Before beginning to question the Appellant about his claim, the panel member told the Appellant to say if he did not know the answer to a question, rather than trying to guess.22 The Appellant then testified that his life is in danger in Mexico. Asked from whom, he said there were two cartels, namely, the Gulf Cartel and the Beltran Leyva Organization.23 When the panel asked the Appellant why he did not mention these groups in his Basis of Claim Form narrative, he said it was because he was not sure.24 The Appellant then acknowledged that he did not know if those cartels were involved and he was speculating.25 I find the Appellant's reference to two specific cartels immediately after being instructed not to guess at his answers undermines the credibility of his allegation that he has been targeted by members of a criminal organization. The Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that a note was left on his sister's body

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding the Appellant's evidence that the alleged agents of persecution left a threatening note on his sister's body was not plausible.26 I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD incorrectly relied on implausibility. There is evidence that organized crime groups in Mexico engage in the practice of leaving messages on women's bodies. However, I find the error non-determinative. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that a note threatening her family was left on his sister's body.

The Appellant's Memorandum states that the Appellant's father identified the body of the Appellant's sister and saw the note but does not refer to evidence supporting this statement.27 I do not find that there is evidence indicating that the Appellant's father saw the note. The Appellant's evidence in his narrative is that his father identified the body and the officer in charge explained the condition in which the body was found, including the message left on her chest saying that her husband had betrayed them and if they went to the police, "another family member" would be next.28 In his testimony, the Appellant explained that his family did not report the incident to the police; rather, when his sister's body was returned to the family, they were told when, how, and where she died.29 The letter from the Appellant's father and the mother of the Appellant's sister in support of the Appellant's claim does not refer to a note nor does it refer to threats against family members.30 The letter states that there was no follow up by the authorities as the authorities received threats from organized crime.31

I find that the evidence does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that a note threatening the Appellant's sister's family was left on her body. The Appellant has also presented no evidence that any member of the Appellant's family or his brother-in-law's family has been harmed since his sister was killed nor has he presented evidence that any family member other than himself has been threatened. The RPD correctly found that the Appellant failed to establish that he received multiple threatening telephone calls, as alleged

The RPD found that the Appellant embellished his evidence about receiving threats.32 The Appellant argues that he was confused at the hearing and that he reasonably explained the inconsistencies in his evidence.33 On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD was correct to conclude that the Appellant has not, on a balance of probabilities, established his allegation that he received threatening phone calls two or three times a week before he left Mexico.

The Appellant's evidence, in his Basis of Claim Form narrative dated October 6, 2019, refers to him receiving a threatening telephone call on the same day that he went to investigating authorities in Chiapas and was told that they had lost his sister's file.34 His evidence is that the call came from someone who: was familiar with the file, told him to drop the investigation, asked about his brother-in-law's whereabouts, and said that, if they continued with the case, another family member would be killed.35 The Appellant states that he hung up and that the phone kept ringing but he did not want to answer.36 In amendments to his narrative, dated March 9, 2020, the Appellant states that before he left for Canada he was receiving threatening phone calls approximately twice or three times a week.37 He states that the callers would say they knew where he and his family lived and, if his family died, it would be the Appellant's fault. The Appellant states that they told him to stop the investigation and if he did not he would be next because they knew where he was.38

At the hearing, the Appellant was asked to explain the difference between his evidence in the initial narrative and in his amended narrative.39 He testified that the calls began when he hired the lawyer. The panel repeated the question and the Appellant testified that the calls started when he started the procedure.40 In later questioning by counsel about why he mentioned only one call in his initial narrative, the Appellant testified that he thought "they got confused when the[y] did the interpretation" and the one call was a reference to the call made by the Appellant's neighbour to tell him that people were walking around his parcel of land and the calls that the Appellant is talking about are the ones he received when he hired the lawyer.41

I have listened to the audio recording of the hearing and I find no indication that the Appellant was confused. His answers to the panel do not respond to the question he was being asked but there is no indication that he did not understand the question. In his answer to counsel, the Appellant suggested that there was a problem with interpretation. The initial narrative is accompanied by an interpreter's declaration indicating that the content was fully interpreted to the Appellant who assured the interpreter that he understood it.42 No evidence has been presented to support the Appellant's suggestion that the interpreter erred. The phone call threatening the Appellant is referred to in paragraph 19 of the initial and amended narratives, and the phone call from the Appellant's neighbour is referred to in paragraph 22 of the initial narrative and paragraph 32 of the amended narrative. I do not see how an error by the interpreter could explain confusion between these events nor how it could explain the omission of the information that the Appellant added in his amended narrative. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant failed to reasonably explain the difference between his initial narrative and his amendments to the narrative and that he embellished his evidence.

The Appellant argues that his evidence is consistent that the threatening phone calls began when he hired the lawyer to investigate his sister's case.43 I do not find that this correctly reflects his evidence. It reflects his testimony at the hearing. However, in his narrative, he states that he received the first call in Chiapas on the day he was told by the authorities that they had lost his sister's file. His evidence in the narrative is that later when he returned to Tabasco, he hired a lawyer.44

I recognize that a claimant has the right to make amendments to their Basis of Claim Form and that this will not necessarily lead to an adverse credibility inference. However, I find there is a significant difference between the evidence of a single threatening phone call on the day the Appellant visited the investigating authorities in Chiapas, and the evidence of two or three threatening phone calls a week between December 2018 and March 2019, when the Appellant left his home in Tabasco to come to Canada. The difference is material to the issue of the motivation of the agent of persecution to pursue the Appellant. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he received the threatening phone calls he alleges that he was receiving in the months before his departure from Mexico. The Appellant's supporting evidence does not establish a continuing threat from his sister's killers

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in failing to consider the evidence from the Mexican lawyer and the neighbour in Mexico and to make a finding contradicting this evidence.45 I am not persuaded by this argument. The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant would be in jeopardy at the hands of the alleged perpetrators of his sister's killing.46 There is no requirement to refer to each piece of evidence or to make specific findings about each piece of evidence tendered in support of a claim. I find that the RPD's reasons reflect a thorough engagement with the evidence. In any event, it is the role of the RAD to conduct an independent assessment, which would remedy the error, had there been one.

The Appellant argues that the letters from the lawyer and the neighbour provide evidence of a continuing threat. The lawyer states that he withdrew from investigating the case of the Appellant's sister's death because he learned that the matter was risky and he advised the Appellant that the matter was wearisome and could cause them problems.47 He does not state the date he withdrew from the matter but the Appellant's evidence is that it was in February 2019.48 The Appellant's neighbour states that, in June 2019, three people in a pickup truck approached him one day, followed by two people on motorcycles days later, in each case asking where and when they could find the Appellant and his family, and in the latter case, offering $1,000 for the information. The Appellant's neighbour states that one of them was communicating through a handheld radio.49 The Appellant's evidence is that the only people who use handheld radios in Mexico are from the government or the cartels.50

I do not find that the lawyer's letter corroborates the Appellant's evidence of a continuing threat. The Appellant's evidence is that the investigating authorities have lost the file, his sister's parents are not pursuing the investigation, the lawyer is not investigating, and the Appellant dropped the matter and would not pursue it again if he were to return to Mexico.51 The evidence is that the Appellant and his family have taken the lawyer's advice.52 The lawyer's letter does not indicate any continuation of a threat following the discontinuation of inquiries and investigation into the sister's death.

I find the neighbour's letter insufficient to support the existence of a threat to the Appellant in the IFA. The Appellant's address history indicates that he lived in XXXX XXXX XXXX Tacotalpa, Tabasco, from XXXX 2001 until his departure from Mexico in XXXX 2019.53 The Appellant refers to the men searching for him after his family had been "relocated within Mexico".54 The Appellant's evidence was that his wife and the children of their relationship continued to reside in Tacotalpa55 and that he rented a farm in Libertad, Tacotalpa.56 The evidence is that the village of Libertad is just over 20 kilometres away from the town of Tacotalpa and is in the municipality Tacotalpa, in the state of Tabasco.57 Information provided by the Appellant indicates that Libertad has a population of 1,042, an increase of 46 people from the year 2005.58 There is no evidence that the men who inquired after the Appellant approached or threatened his family in Tabasco.

When the Appellant was questioned about the threat he alleged was included in the note on his sister's body, he was asked if cartel members who allegedly killed his sister took any action against any member of the family after his sister's death was reported to the police. He testified that the threat was more towards him.59 His testimony was that they did not carry out their threat because he moved.60 The evidence does not indicate when the Appellant and his family moved. I accept the Appellant's evidence that he moved but the evidence is that he did not move far. The Appellant has not alleged that he lived in hiding between the date of his sister's death in April 2017 and his departure for Canada in XXXX 2019.

I find that the Appellant has not established that whoever killed his sister is motivated to locate him in Merida or Campeche, given that there is no evidence that they located him before he left Mexico while he continued to live in an area with a population of just over one thousand people where he had lived for almost 18 years. The Appellant's evidence does not establish that his sister's killers are motivated to pursue him despite the absence of an investigation into her death

The Appellant's evidence is that the investigation into his sister's death was discontinued and, according to the Appellant, is not being pursued by authorities or family members. The Appellant's counsel asked him why the cartel would still pursue him, given that there is no longer any investigation. He testified that there are two reasons. One reason is because he can identify two men who attended his sister's funeral and he believes they are connected to his sister's killing. The other is that the cartels want to find his brother-in-law and they think the Appellant knows his brother-in-law's whereabouts.61

I find the Appellant's evidence that cartel members would pursue him because they fear he could identify people connected to his sister's death is speculative. The Appellant testified that two men who attended his sister's funeral told him they were friends of the family. He testified that they asked when the Appellant's brother-in-law would arrive and asked why there were police and journalists at the funeral.62 The Appellant's evidence is that he subsequently recognized their faces in a video shown to him by the police.63 He testified that he thinks they are the assassins.64 His testimony was that they were in a truck that was outside his sister's house in the morning of the day that his sister was killed in the afternoon.65 The Appellant testified that he saw the video two or three months after his sister died, he could not see their faces exactly, but he knew it was them because they were in the same truck.66

The Appellant's evidence is that the police are no longer investigating the killing of the Appellant's sister.67 The Appellant alleges that the police have dropped the investigation because of the cartel's influence. Consequently, I find it speculative that his ability to identify two guests at the funeral as people who were in a truck outside his sister's home on the morning of the day she later died would motivate cartel members, who allegedly killed his sister, to look for the Appellant in the IFA.

The Appellant also testified that he fears the cartel wants to locate him because they think he knows the whereabouts of his brother-in-law.68 He testified that if he had not told the authorities in December 2018 that his brother-in-law would continue to pursue the investigation, his life would not be in danger.69 I find this speculative and inconsistent with the Appellant's argument that he cannot live safely in an IFA location because cartel members can locate him anywhere in Mexico.

I agree with the Appellant that there is evidence that, in many cases, cartel members are able to locate people when they are motivated to do so. The Appellant's evidence is that he is not sure of his brother-in-law's real name as he used several names, because of his ties to the cartel and gangs in Mexico.70 According to the Appellant, he and his family did not know about his brother-in-law's activities.71 His evidence is that they learned of his involvement in human trafficking only after the Appellant's sister was killed.72 The evidence is that it is more likely cartel members know more about the Appellant's brother-in-law than the Appellant does.

The only evidence the Appellant has provided in support of his allegation that cartel members think he knows his brother-in-law's whereabouts is that in December 2018 he told the investigating authorities that his brother-in-law would pursue the investigation.73 I find that this does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that cartel members believe the Appellant knows where his brother-in-law is. To reach that conclusion requires assuming that the authorities relayed that information to cartel members, that the cartel members believed that the Appellant was telling the truth about being in contact with his brother-in-law, and that the cartel members believed that the Appellant's brother-in-law had disclosed his location to the Appellant. This chain of reasoning requires a series of speculative assumptions. I am required to base my findings on the evidence and I find that the Appellant has not presented evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the conclusions that I would need to reach to accept his argument.

The Appellant also argues that individuals found the Appellant's family in the location where they had sought safety in Mexico.74 As I have already explained, his family remained in the same small municipality where the Appellant had been living for almost 18 years. I accept that the cartel members would likely be able to locate him in that municipality, if they were motivated to do so. I find the absence of any evidence that they located him before he left Mexico or that they approached his family indicative of a lack of interest in the Appellant and his family. The evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that his sister's killers are motivated to locate the Appellant

I accept the evidence that cartels in Mexico have many ways to locate people, when they are motivated to do so. I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that whoever killed his sister, allegedly members of a cartel or organized crime group, are motivated to locate him in an IFA. The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that XXXX has the means and the motivation to locate the Appellant in Mexico in order to harm him

The Appellant alleges that he fears XXXX, a former supervisor in a Canadian workplace. His evidence is that, after he arrived in Canada, XXXX got him a job with a XXXX XXXX and a place to live, although the Appellant did not have a work permit. The Appellant's evidence is that XXXX deceived him about Canadian immigration rules. The Appellant made a connection through his church with a refugee centre and a lawyer and encouraged other migrants not to give XXXX their money and not to follow his advice. As a result, XXXX threatened the Appellant and fired him from his job. The Appellant reported XXXX and his business to the police.75 In December 2020, the Appellant heard from former co-workers that XXXX was upset and asking around for the Appellant's contact information. The Appellant has been told that there are rumours circulating in the local Mexican community that the employer for whom the XXXX XXXX provided services was fined because of an investigation involving the Appellant and XXXX was upset that this would have an impact on his business.76 For the purposes of the analysis, I accept these allegations.

The Appellant alleges that he will not be safe in Mexico because XXXX seeks to do him harm. The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence to show that XXXX has the ability or the interest to pursue the Appellant and his family in Mexico.77 The Appellant argues that the evidence of XXXX continued interest in him would potentially justify accepting his claim.78 I find no error in the RPD's conclusion. I have considered the new evidence submitted to the RAD, and on an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established that XXXX has the ability to locate or harm the Appellant in an IFA location in Mexico.

Counsel's submissions to the RPD acknowledged that it was unclear whether the Appellant faces risk from XXXX in Mexico and that it was unknown whether XXXX actually has any connections to anyone in Mexico who could harm the Appellant's family.79 I agree. The evidence that XXXX has recently asked for the Appellant's contact information in Canada and is upset about possible business losses that he attributes to the Appellant does not address those gaps in the evidence. The evidence XXXX Jorge is upset with the Appellant does not assist the Appellant to establish means by which XXXX could harm the Appellant in an IFA location in Mexico. The RPD correctly found that the Appellant has not established that, on a balance of probabilities, it would be unreasonable for him to relocate to Merida or Campeche

The RPD found that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to one of the proposed IFA locations.80 The Appellant argues that it was an error for the RPD to find that there is an IFA in Merida or Campeche.81 On an independent assessment, for the reasons that follow, I agree with the RPD's conclusion that the evidence does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that it would be unreasonable for the Appellant to go and live in Merida or Campeche.

The Appellant was asked if he could live safely in Merida or Campeche. He testified that where his sister died is seven hours from Campeche and where he lived is four hours from Campeche and the whole area is very dangerous.82 The RPD considered the evidence that crime in Merida and Campeche had increased but noted that country conditions documentation indicates that it is generally low in the area. The Appellant argues that the RAD's recent jurisprudence supports that Campeche and Merida are not free from violence but are places where claimants who have been targeted may be found.83 As the RPD also noted, it is not necessary that an IFA be free of crime; that is not the test. While administrative tribunals strive to promote consistency in decision-making, each appeal is decided on its own facts. Furthermore, the decision cited by the Appellant deals with the ability of the Jalisco Cartel New Generation to locate a claimant whom the cartel is motivated to pursue. For the reasons I have already given, I find that the Appellant has not established that he would be pursued by cartel members.

The Appellant's submissions focus on the safety of the IFA locations. The Appellant made no other submissions at the RPD or the RAD about reasonableness of the IFAs. The RPD considered that the Appellant is a young man with work experience and concluded that it was not objectively unreasonable for him to move to one of the IFA locations, to be eventually joined by his wife and children. On an independent assessment, I come to the same conclusion as the RPD, namely that it is not objectively unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Campeche or Merida.

I dismiss the appeal and pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
